   WRC-27 AGENDA ITEM 1.13 - CONSIDERATIONS ON COMPATIBILITY
 STUDY BETWEEN EESS IN THE FREQUENCY BAND 2 200-2 290 MHZ (S-E)
   AND DC-MSS-IMT OPERATING IN THE FREQUENCY BAND 2 110-2 200
                                          (DOWNLINK)



Introduction
Following the structure adopted during the previous Working Party 4C (WP 4C) meeting for studies
under WRC-27 agenda item 1.13, the Brazilian Administration is reviewing and providing the
required sharing and compatibility studies.


Proposal
Brazil proposes an update to Study B in of the attachment a compatibility study between the Earth
Exploration-Satellite Service (EESS) (s-E) in the frequency band 2 200-2 290 MHz and Direct
Connectivity-Mobile Satellite Service-International Mobile Telecommunications (DC-MSS-IMT)
operating in the frequency band 2 110-2 200 MHz to be added to Annex 4 of Working Document on
sharing and compatibility studies under WRC-27 agenda item 1.13 (Annex 7 to Doc. 4C/356).

A4.3.1.2      Study B (4C/427 (B))
The purpose of this study is to assess the interference from the usage of MSS for direct connectivity
between space stations and International Mobile Telecommunications (IMT) equipment (DC-MSS-
IMT) into EESS (s-E) operating in the frequency bands 2 200‑2 290 MHz. This frequency band is
adjacent to the frequency band 2 110‑2 200 MHz.
This study assesses the interference from space-to-Earth (downlink) transmissions of non-
geostationary (non-GSO) DC-MSS-IMT systems into EESS (s-E) earth station receivers operating in
the frequency band 2 200-2 290 MHz, considering various use cases and simulation scenarios.
The compatibility scenarios between DC-MSS-IMT and EESS under study are in accordance with
Document 4C/356, as well as with Document 4C/196, which describe parameters of EESS systems
of interest to WP 7C and WP 7B, respectively. We have considered two different DC-MSS-IMT
coverage scenarios interfering on EESS earth station in two different positions:
CASE I: this scenario involves the downlink operation of a DC-MSS-IMT system covering South
America, and an EESS system operating in the space-to-Earth (s-E) direction, referred to as case I.
Two earth station positions are evaluated: in Paraguay (25°55’S 54°57′49″W) and in Colombia
(4°21’S 69°55′W), as shown in Figure A4.3.1.2-1 (a).
CASE II: The second scenario (Case II) is examined in the study within the context of four South
American countries: the DC-MSS-IMT system has authorization to operate in Brazil and Argentina,
while it does not have authorization in Paraguay and Colombia, where an EESS system operates in
the adjacent frequency band to the DC-MSS-IMT system (Figure A4.3.1.2-1 (b)).
It is important to note that, given the broad applicability of the adopted methodology, the study could
have been conducted for any location on the globe and is therefore of interest to other administrations.
Furthermore, the simulations use EESS earth station parameters proposed by other countries
(Document 4C/196), which provides representativeness to this study.

criterion for the incumbent victim system.

A4.3.1.2.1    Technical and operational characteristics of DC-MSS-IMT operating in the
              frequency band 2 110-2 200 MHz
We analyze a representative non-GSO DC-MSS-IMT system (System 3, Annex 1, Document 4C/356).
The relevant orbital and technical characteristics for this system are based on the parameters provided
in Annex 1 to the working document on WRC-27 agenda item 1.13 (Annex 7 to Document 4C/356).
In this contribution, we have selected System 3 at 525 km and 340 km altitudes.
The parameters of System 3 are presented in Table A4.3.2.2-1, extracted from Document 4C/356.
Moreover, the EIRP is kept constant on the satellite, and the resulting PFD on the ground depends
on the elevation angle.

It is noted that the System3 characteristics specify the reference antenna with a fixed diameter and
assume a wavelength of 0.15 m, irrespective of the actual system operating frequency. This
formulation may not fully reflect frequency-dependent behavior when modelling systems in different

Protection Criterion
Regarding protection criterion, Recommendation ITU-R SA.514 specifies that, for space-to-Earth
data transmission links in frequency bands not addressed by Recommendations ITU-R SA.1026, ITU-
R SA.1160, and ITU-R SA.1163, the interference criteria for Earth receiving sites operating between
1 and 10 GHz is: the power spectral density of noise interference, or the total power of continuous
wave (CW)-type interference in any single band or combination of bands, must not exceed -154
dB(W/MHz) at the receiver input for more than 1% of the time.

A4.3.1.2.4    Methodology

A4.3.1.2.4.1           Interference Scenario
As mentioned, this study analyzes, as Case I, all South American countries covered by the DC-MSS-
IMT system, with an EESS system receiver positioned in the center of Brazil. The DC-MSS-IMT
system and the EESS system operate in an adjacent frequency band.
In Case II, a specific cross-border interference scenario is analyzed, which is a concrete and
representative implementation of the generalized case described in the working document. For this
analysis, a hypothetical deployment is assumed where a DC-MSS-IMT system is fully operational,
providing service over Brazil’s and Argentina’s territories. The victim under analysis comprises an
EESS receiver, located in Paraguay and Colombia, and positioned at a representative point along its
border with Brazil. Case II also includes an interference-mitigation feature, defined here as an
operational margin (service margin).
To model an operational approach for managing cross-border interference, this analysis incorporates
a service margin from the political borders (Figures A4.3.1.2-6), in the study Case II. This margin
defines a distance from the border within the territories of Brazil and Argentina where the center of
the DC-MSS satellite beams shall not be pointed. This operational constraint creates a beam-pointing
exclusion zone, ensuring that the high-gain main lobe of any satellite beam is directed only within
the licensed country. As a result, the interference received by the victim EESS earth station (ES) in
Paraguay is primarily composed of side-lobe emissions, representing a practical mitigation technique
that DC-MSS operators could implement.
This scenario was specifically chosen to evaluate the aggregate interference from multiple DC-MSS-
IMT systems operating in neighboring countries into the territory of a third country where the service
is not deployed, representing a realistic challenge for cross-border coordination.
The operational margin does not exist in Case I of this study; therefore, the satellite beams can be
directed toward any region within the South American continent.  All simulations presented in this
study were conducted using the SHARC (SHARing and Compatibility study) software tool. This
open-source simulator is publicly available for review and result replication at the following web
address: https://github.com/Radio-Spectrum/SHARC.

Adjacent channel interference model and spurious emissions
The channel bandwidth for the interfering DC‑MSS-IMT downlink (DC‑MSS‑DL) was assumed to
be 5 MHz in the band 2 110-2 200 MHz of System 3. The victim EESS earth station system operates
in the band 2 200-2 290 MHz. Moreover, it is assumed that the DC-MSS-IMT system transmits
signals under two scenarios (see Figure A4.3.1.2-7):
(1) at f2 = 2 117.5 MHz, with a channel bandwidth of 5 MHz, while the EESS system operates in the
frequency range 2 200-2 204 MHz, with a channel bandwidth of 4 MHz (System B), representing a
spurious emissions interference case;
(2) at f2 = 2 117.5 MHz, with a channel bandwidth of 5 MHz, while the EESS system operates in the
frequency range 2 200-2 206 MHz, with a channel bandwidth of 6 MHz (System D), representing a
spurious emissions interference case.
For the spurious emission, we have adopted a value of -13 dBm/MHz.

Interference Calculation Methodology
The total interference power at the victim EESS earth station receiver is calculated as the aggregate
sum of the power received from all individual DC-MSS satellites that are visible from the receiver’s
location (i.e., above its minimum elevation angle of 5 degrees).
For each snapshot in the Monte Carlo simulation, the interference power received by the earth
station from a single satellite i, denoted as Ii (in dBW), is calculated using the following formula:
                                            Ii=   EIR   Pi(θt )- L  pi+Gr   (θr) ,
where EIR     Pi  (θt) is the Equivalent Isotropically Radiated Power of the interfering satellite i in the
direction of the EESS earth station receiver. EIR             Pi  (θt) considers if the victim is at
adjacent‑channel interference conditions as illustrated in Figure A4.3.1.1‑8. In this sense, it is
calculated by integrating the emission spectrum mask shown in Figure A4.3.1.1‑9, over the specific
frequency bands assigned to earth station. The value of EIR                 Pi  (θt ) is a function of the satellite’s
transmit antenna gain at the specific off-axis angle (θt) towards the victim receiver. Finally, L                       pi is
the total propagation path loss between satellite i and earth station receiver, calculated in
accordance with the appropriate ITU-R P-series Recommendations, and Gr(θr                           )  is the receive
antenna gain of the receiver in the direction of the interfering satellite i, determined by the signal’s
angle of arrival (θr).
According to Document 4C/356, the antenna radiation pattern may be modeled using ITU-R
Recommendation S.1528, and for the immediately adjacent channels, the same pattern is considered
more appropriate.
For each snapshot in the Monte Carlo simulation, the aggregate interference power, Iagg, from all N                            s
visible satellites, is then determined by the linear summation of the power received from each
individual satellite:

A4.3.1.2.4.2            Non-GSO Constellation Modelling
The NGSO constellations were modelled based on their defined Keplerian elements, including
altitude, inclination, and the number of orbital planes and the number of satellites per plane.
To perform the statistical analysis independent of a specific time epoch, a snapshot-based Monte
Carlo methodology was employed. In this approach, instead of propagating the satellite positions
over a time-based simulation, the initial orbital angles for each satellite in the constellation were
randomized. Specifically, a reference satellite and orbital plane are defined. The mean anomaly (M)
of this satellite within its orbital plane and the right ascension of the ascending node (RAAN, Ω) of
that orbital plane (Figure A4.3.1.2-8) are modeled as independent random variables uniformly
distributed over [0°, 360°]. In each snapshot of the Monte Carlo process, the values of M and Ω are
randomly drawn, and the orbital positions of the remaining satellites and orbital planes are then
determined in accordance with the orbital parameters of the DC-MSS-IMT system, as listed in
Table A4.3.1.2-1.


                                                    FIGURE A4.3.1.2-8
                                                    Orbit plane angles























This method generates a statistically representative snapshot of the entire constellation’s geometry
at each simulation run. By repeating this process over many iterations, it is possible to accurately
capture the statistical distribution of interference without the computational overhead and time-
dependency of a full dynamic simulation, making it an efficient and effective approach for this type
of study. A total of 10,000 snapshots were generated in this study, providing a sufficient sample
size for statistical convergence.

A4.3.1.2.4.3           Satellite Beam Generation and Pointing Methodology


                                                   FIGURE A4.3.1.2-9
                                               Satellite beam assignment
















To model the service deployment for the DC-MSS-IMT systems, a Service Grid methodology was
employed to generate and point satellite beams (Figures A4.3.1.2-9 and A4.3.1.2-10). This method
ensures that continuous coverage is provided throughout the intended service area while adhering to
operational constraints.
The process is defined by the following steps:
1)            Service Grid Generation
The defined service area is tessellated into a grid of contiguous, non-overlapping hexagonal-cells
(Figure A4.3.1.1-9), whose centers are illustrated in Figure A4.3.1.1-10. The radius of each
hexagonal-cell is set to be equal to the coverage radius of a single satellite beam, R in the Figure
A4.3.1.1-4, ensuring that one beam can effectively serve one hexagonal-cell. These hexagonal
structures were used for illustrative purposes, with R, as described earlier in this document, being the
most relevant element of the proposed methodology. In this study, R is set to 40.448 km and 26.195
km for the analysis of System 3, at altitudes of 525 km and 340 km, respectively, along the -7 dB
contour of each beam's radiation pattern.
The presented service grid in Figure A4.3.1.1-11 considers only the South American countries in
which the service points are covered by DC-MSS-IMT satellites that allow visibility with the EESS
earth station under study.

2)             Definition of the Service Area
The service area, which comprises all the (hexagonal) cells eligible to be served, is defined at each
snapshot by a set of operational and geographical constraints. A satellite beam can only be placed
within a cell if the following three conditions are met simultaneously:
–              The hexagon is located entirely within the political borders of the country licensed to
               operate the service (e.g., Brazil), respecting the pre-defined grid limits from the
               international border (Figure A4.3.1.2-10).
–              The hexagonal-cell is within the visibility footprint of at least one satellite in the
               constellation.
–              The satellite whose beam covers a cell is visible from the specific victim ground station
               under study, allowing for the calculation of the interference path. Visibility is defined
               by a minimum elevation angle, which in this study was set to 5 degrees, in accordance
               with Document 4C/356.
3)             Beam Assignment and Pointing
For each hexagonal-cell within the defined service area, a single beam is assigned based on the best
server principle. The satellite with the highest elevation angle as seen from the center of that
hexagonal cell is selected to provide service. This satellite then points the main lobe of one of its
beams directly to the center of the assigned hexagon. This methodology ensures that the entire
service area is systematically covered by the assigned beams, utilizing the satellite with the most
favorable link geometry for each cell (Figure A4.3.1.2-11).

Figure A4.3.1.2-11 illustrates a snapshot of the Monte Carlo process. In this figure, the green points
represent a subset of the satellites of System 3 that can cover the cells of the service grid in the

The satellite beam size is defined by its average service contour at the 7 dB power falloff point from
the peak gain of the main lobe. This definition is used to implement an exclusive beam layout,
where adjacent beams are placed no closer than their respective 7 dB contours. This 7 dB value
must be derived using the specific antenna radiation pattern described in model 1.4 of
Recommendation ITU-R S.1528.

4)            Satellite system load factor
To model realistic network usage, a satellite system load factor was applied, defining the probability
that any given beam is active and transmitting during a single simulation snapshot; for this analysis,
load factors of 20% and 50% were considered.
Figures A4.3.1.2-12 and A4.3.1.2-13 present the frequency histograms of the number of active
beams per satellite, for system load factors of 20% and 50%, respectively. These distributions were
generated from a simulation comprising 10,000 independent snapshots.

A4.3.1.2.5    Results of the study
This study addresses an adjacent-channel interference scenario involving the DC-MSS-IMT
(downlink) system and EESS (s-E) system.
As previously mentioned, DC-MSS-IMT System 3 is considered in the study. Two altitude levels for
System 3 are employed for comparison purposes: 340km and 525km. The study includes an analysis
of the DC-MSS-IMT system load factor, assuming load factors of 20% and 50%.
Case I – The whole of South America is covered by the DC-MSS system. Results of adjacent-
band interference and spurious emission interference caused to the EESS (s-E) system B and D

in the band 2 200-2 290 MHz by the DC-MSS-IMT system operating in the 2 110-2 200 MHz
band (downlink)
In this case, two victim EESS earth stations located in Paraguay and Colombia are evaluated, as
illustrated in Figure A4.3.1.2-1 (a). However, in each snapshot, the elevation and azimuth angles of
the receiving antenna are randomly selected, reflecting the receiving antenna's tracking capability
during communication with an NGSO satellite. These elevation and azimuth angles are modeled as
independent random variables uniformly distributed over the ranges 5 to 90 degrees and 0 to 360
degrees, respectively.

A4.3.1.2.6    Conclusion of study B
The results of this study indicate that coexistence between EESS (s-E) systems operating in the 2
200–2 290 MHz band and DC-MSS-IMT downlink systems operating in the 2 110–2 200 MHz band
is feasible under the considered spurious emission conditions.
For the 340 km case, some scenarios without the application of an operational margin around the
EESS earth station and with a load factor of 50% exceed the protection criterion of -154 dBW/MHz.
However, the introduction of a protection margin around the EESS station is sufficient to mitigate the
interference and ensure compliance in all evaluated scenarios.
Overall, the results demonstrate that, with appropriate mitigation measures, particularly the
application of a protection margin around the EESS earth station, DC-MSS operation in the 2 110–2
120 MHz band is compatible with EESS systems.
